questions.question: What is the difference between @Mock and @Spy in Mockito?
questions.title: @Mock vs @Spy Mockito | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **@Mock creates a fully fake object** — all methods return default values (null, 0, false) unless stubbed. **@Spy wraps a real object** — unstubbed methods call the real implementation; only configured methods are overridden. Use @Spy when you want to test a real object but control some behaviors.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Mockito knowledge — choosing the right tool
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @Spy when a full @Mock would be cleaner, or not understanding that @Spy calls real methods by default
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete use case: @Spy is useful for partial mocking of legacy code you can't easily refactor

sections.title: Fake vs Wrapped Real Object
sections.content: **@Mock**: completely fake — no real method calls. `list.size()` returns 0, `repository.findById(1)` returns null. You must stub everything you want to return a meaningful value. **@Spy**: `@Spy List<String> spyList = new ArrayList<>()` — `spyList.add("a")` actually adds to the list. `spyList.size()` actually returns 1. But you can stub specific methods: `doReturn(10).when(spyList).size()`. Use @Spy for testing a class where most logic is real but you want to stub one method.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- @Mock: fake, all methods stubbed to defaults or configured
- @Spy: wraps real object, unstubbed methods call real impl
- @Spy requires: existing instance or no-arg constructor
- Use doReturn().when() for @Spy (not when().thenReturn() — can trigger real method)
- @Spy use case: partial mock for legacy code
- @Mock is the default choice — @Spy is the exception
- @Spy can verify interactions just like @Mock
- InjectMocks works with both @Mock and @Spy

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @Mock creates a completely fake object where all methods return default values — null for objects, zero for numbers, false for booleans — unless explicitly stubbed. @Spy wraps a real object, so unstubbed methods call the real implementation while you can still override specific methods. For example, a spy on an ArrayList actually adds elements when you call add, unlike a mock which would do nothing. I use @Mock for dependencies where I want full control and @Spy for legacy classes where most methods should execute real code but I need to override one or two behaviors. The important detail with @Spy is to use doReturn-when instead of when-thenReturn to avoid triggering the real method during stubbing setup.

questions.question: What is a test double and what are the different types?
questions.title: Test Double Types | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Test doubles are fake objects that replace real dependencies in tests.** Types: **Dummy** (placeholder, unused), **Stub** (returns canned values), **Fake** (working simpler implementation), **Mock** (verifies interactions), **Spy** (wraps real object). Gerard Meszaros coined these terms.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using 'mock' for every type of test double — shows lack of depth
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete example for each type and connect to Mockito's implementation

sections.title: Five Types of Test Doubles
sections.content: **Dummy**: passed but never used — `null` or empty object to satisfy method signature. **Stub**: returns configured answers — `when(repo.find(1)).thenReturn(user)`. **Fake**: working simplified implementation — in-memory HashMap database. **Mock**: records and verifies interactions — `verify(emailService).send(any())`. **Spy**: wraps a real object — partial mocking. All Mockito `@Mock` objects are technically mock+stub hybrids; Mockito `@Spy` is a spy.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Dummy: never actually used, fills parameter requirement
- Stub: state-focused, returns configured values
- Fake: real logic, but simpler (in-memory DB, embedded H2)
- Mock: interaction-focused, verifies method calls
- Spy: partial mock — real + some stubbed
- Mockito covers: stub, mock, spy
- Fake example: H2 in-memory database, Spring's MockMvc
- In practice: 'mock' is used loosely for all types

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Gerard Meszaros defined five test double types. A dummy is just a placeholder that satisfies a parameter signature but is never used. A stub returns configured values when called. A fake is a simplified working implementation like an in-memory database. A mock records interactions for verification. A spy wraps a real object and delegates to it unless specific methods are stubbed. In Mockito, @Mock objects are stubs and mocks combined — you can both configure return values and verify calls on them. @Spy implements the spy concept. In conversation developers usually say 'mock' for all of these, which is fine as long as you can explain the distinctions when asked.

questions.question: What is @InjectMocks in Mockito and how does it work?
questions.title: @InjectMocks Mockito Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **@InjectMocks creates an instance of the class under test and injects @Mock and @Spy fields into it.** It uses constructor injection first, then setter injection, then field injection. It saves writing `new ClassUnderTest(mockDep1, mockDep2)` in every test.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) which is required for @InjectMocks to work
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the injection strategy order: constructor → setter → field, and note the gotcha that @InjectMocks silently does nothing if injection fails

sections.title: Automatic Dependency Injection in Tests
sections.content: `@InjectMocks OrderService orderService` — Mockito creates `new OrderService()` and injects all `@Mock` and `@Spy` fields in the test class. **Injection order**: (1) Constructor injection (preferred — matches constructor parameters by type). (2) Setter injection. (3) Field injection (least preferred). **Gotcha**: if injection fails, Mockito creates the object but silently doesn't inject — the field may be null, causing NullPointerException at runtime.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- @InjectMocks: creates instance + injects @Mock/@Spy fields
- Requires: @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
- Injection order: constructor → setter → field
- Silent failure: if no match, injects null without error
- Prefers constructor injection — works with Spring's @Service pattern
- @Spy fields are also injected by @InjectMocks
- Limitations: can't inject into final fields, primitive constructor args
- Alternative: manual construction new Service(mockRepo, mockEmailService)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @InjectMocks tells Mockito to create an instance of the class under test and inject all the @Mock and @Spy fields declared in the test class into it. Mockito tries constructor injection first — it matches mocks to constructor parameters by type. If that doesn't work, it tries setter injection, then field injection. This saves me from writing new OrderService with all the mock parameters in every @BeforeEach. The one gotcha is that if Mockito can't inject a dependency, it fails silently and the field may be null — causing a NullPointerException in the test rather than a helpful error message.

questions.question: How do you use doReturn().when() vs when().thenReturn() in Mockito?
questions.title: doReturn vs when thenReturn Mockito | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: **Both stub a method, but `doReturn().when()` avoids calling the real method during setup.** For `@Mock` objects, both work the same. For `@Spy` objects, `when().thenReturn()` calls the real method before stubbing, which can cause side effects or exceptions. Use `doReturn().when()` with spies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Subtlety of Mockito API and when each form is appropriate
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using when().thenReturn() on a @Spy and triggering the real method during stub setup
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the execution sequence: when(spy.method()) executes the real method to record the call before thenReturn is set

sections.title: The Spy Gotcha
sections.content: `when(mock.getValue()).thenReturn(5)` — works fine for @Mock (no real method called). `when(spy.getValue()).thenReturn(5)` — **calls `spy.getValue()` during setup**, then applies the stub. If `getValue()` throws an exception or has side effects, your test setup breaks. **Safe form for Spy**: `doReturn(5).when(spy).getValue()` — configures the stub WITHOUT calling the real method. Also preferred for void methods: `doNothing().when(mock).voidMethod()`, `doThrow().when(mock).method()`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- when().thenReturn(): fine for @Mock, risky for @Spy
- doReturn().when(): safe for @Spy (no real method call)
- doThrow().when(): stub to throw exception
- doNothing().when(): stub void method
- doAnswer().when(): complex stubbing with logic
- doCallRealMethod().when(): call real method on mock
- BDD style alternative: given().willReturn() (same as when().thenReturn())

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Both forms stub a method's return value, but the execution differs. With when-thenReturn, Mockito actually calls the method to record the invocation before applying the stub — for a @Mock this is fine because no real code runs. For a @Spy, this calls the real implementation during setup, which can throw an exception or cause side effects that break your test setup before it even starts. So with @Spy I always use doReturn-when, which directly configures the stub without triggering the real method. doThrow and doNothing are the equivalent forms for stubbing exceptions and void methods.

questions.question: When would you use a Spy instead of a Mock?
questions.title: When to Use a Spy
questions.direct_answer: Use a Spy when you want to call the real methods of an object by default but selectively stub or verify only specific methods.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that a Spy wraps a real object and when partial stubbing is appropriate
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a Spy everywhere instead of only when real method execution for untouched methods is specifically needed
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that doReturn() must be used instead of when().thenReturn() on a Spy to avoid calling the real method during stubbing

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
A Spy in Mockito wraps a real, instantiated object. By default every method call on a Spy executes the real implementation, unlike a Mock which returns null or zero by default. You would choose a Spy when you want most of the real behavior but need to stub or verify just one or two specific methods.

A common use case is testing a class that has a method calling an external service. You create a Spy of the class, let all the business logic methods run for real, and stub only the method that makes the external call. This is also useful when you are refactoring legacy code that does not have a clean dependency injection structure yet.

One important detail: when stubbing a Spy you should use doReturn().when() instead of when().thenReturn(). With when().thenReturn() the real method gets invoked during the stubbing setup itself, which can cause unintended side effects or errors. doReturn() bypasses the real call.

That said, over-using Spies is a design smell. If you frequently need a Spy it often means your class has too many responsibilities. A well-designed class should be fully testable with pure Mocks and injected dependencies.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Spy wraps a real object; unstubbed methods call the real implementation
Mock returns null/zero by default; all methods are replaced
Use Spy for partial mocking — real logic with one or two stubbed methods
Use doReturn().when(spy) not when(spy).thenReturn() to avoid triggering real method during stub setup

questions.question: What is a Fake object and how does it differ from a Mock?
questions.title: Fake Object vs Mock
questions.direct_answer: A Fake is a working but simplified implementation used for testing (like an in-memory database), while a Mock is framework-generated and focuses on verifying interactions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the broader vocabulary of test doubles beyond just what Mockito provides
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Fakes with Mocks; Fakes have real logic, Mocks have expectation-based logic
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete example like H2 for database faking or a simple HashMap-backed fake repository

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
A Fake is a hand-written, working implementation of a dependency that is simpler or faster than the real thing but still contains real logic. The classic example is H2, an in-memory relational database. It is not the real PostgreSQL you use in production, but it genuinely processes SQL, enforces constraints, and stores data — it is a working substitute, not a mock. Another example is a fake email service that stores sent emails in a List instead of actually sending them, so your tests can assert what was sent without network calls.

A Mock, by contrast, is generated at runtime by a framework like Mockito. It has no real behavior — you explicitly program what it returns and what interactions you expect. The Mock's purpose is interaction verification: did my service call the repository once with the right arguments?

The tradeoff is effort versus realism. Fakes take more work to write and maintain but they behave more like the real thing, giving you higher confidence. Mocks are quick to set up but only test the narrow contract you define in your stubs.

In practice, use Fakes for dependencies where the real behavior matters to your test correctness, and use Mocks when you only care about whether a method was called.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Fake = working simplified implementation (H2, in-memory list repository)
Mock = framework-generated object with stubbed returns and interaction verification
Fakes require more effort but give higher confidence in real behavior
Use Fakes when the logic of the dependency matters; use Mocks when only the interaction matters

questions.question: Can you spy on a final class or a static method in Mockito, and how?
questions.title: Mocking Final Classes and Static Methods
questions.direct_answer: Yes — since Mockito 2.x with the inline mock maker extension, you can mock and spy on final classes and stub static methods using mockStatic().

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Mockito's extended capabilities and their caveats
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Mockito can never mock final classes or static methods
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that heavy use of static mocking often signals a design problem and suggest refactoring via wrapper classes or dependency injection instead

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Classic Mockito uses subclassing under the hood, which means it cannot mock final classes, final methods, or static methods — these cannot be overridden. However, Mockito 2 introduced the inline mock maker, and Mockito 4 and 5 include it by default (or via the mockito-inline artifact in older versions). The inline mock maker uses the Java Instrumentation API to rewrite bytecode at runtime, bypassing the subclassing limitation.

To mock a final class you just call Mockito.mock(FinalClass.class) as normal when inline mode is active. To mock static methods, you use a try-with-resources block: try (MockedStatic<ClassName> mocked = Mockito.mockStatic(ClassName.class)) { mocked.when(ClassName::staticMethod).thenReturn(value); ... }. The try-with-resources ensures the static mock is closed and the original behaviour is restored after the block.

That said, needing to mock static methods or final classes is usually a design smell. Static calls create hidden, untestable dependencies. The cleaner solution is to wrap the static call in an instance method of a small collaborator class, inject that collaborator, and mock the collaborator normally. For example, instead of calling LocalDate.now() directly, inject a Clock or a DateProvider interface. This makes the design more flexible and eliminates the need for inline mocking entirely.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Mockito's inline mock maker enables mocking of final classes, final methods, and static methods.
Use Mockito.mockStatic() in a try-with-resources block to mock static calls.
Static mocking must be closed after the test to restore original behaviour.
Prefer refactoring static calls behind an injectable interface over using mockStatic().
